# Build a Static Website with HTML and CSS {#sec-ch02}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[WEB 02 | Game Maker HQ]{.game-title}

[HTML]{.skill-chip} [CSS]{.skill-chip} [Forms]{.skill-chip} [Page structure]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- make an HTML page and connect a CSS file to it
- use headings, sections, lists, and classes to give a page structure
- use basic CSS rules, selectors, and declarations
- change font family, size, weight, and style to give a site its voice
- style a local image with size, borders, rounded corners, and a shadow
- add labeled text, menu, checkbox, and button input elements

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

HTML says what belongs on a page. CSS says how it should look. Together they make a static website—the visual stage that JavaScript will make interactive in the next chapter.

:::

## Make the project folder

Create the folder from Chapter 1 and open it in your text editor:

```
my-game-site/
  index.html
  styles.css
  gem.svg
```

Keep the files in the same folder. The HTML file will use a `<link>` element to tell the browser where to find the CSS file. Copy [gem.svg](../games/assets/2d/gem.svg) from this textbook into your new folder so the page can show a local image.

## Build the page with HTML

Save this complete example as `index.html`. HTML tags use angle brackets. Most tags have an opening tag and a matching closing tag; the content goes between them.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Game Maker HQ</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <main class="card">
    <p class="eyebrow">MY STATIC WEBSITE</p>
    <h1>Game Maker HQ</h1>
    <p class="intro">Plan the next game you want to build.</p>

    <section class="game-preview">
      <img class="game-art" src="gem.svg"
           alt="A shiny purple gem for a game treasure.">
      <div>
        <h2>Gem Quest</h2>
        <p>Collect three gems, then open the portal.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section>
      <h2>Today's missions</h2>
      <ul>
        <li>Sketch one game character.</li>
        <li>Choose a goal for the player.</li>
        <li>Invent a fair challenge.</li>
      </ul>
    </section>

    <section>
      <h2>Player card</h2>
      <form>
        <label for="player-name">Your game-maker name</label>
        <input id="player-name" name="player-name" type="text"
               placeholder="Type a nickname">

        <label for="game-type">Game type</label>
        <select id="game-type" name="game-type">
          <option>Adventure</option>
          <option>Puzzle</option>
          <option>Sports</option>
        </select>

        <label class="check-row" for="sound-on">
          <input id="sound-on" name="sound-on" type="checkbox">
          I want sound effects in my game.
        </label>

        <button type="button">My game will use this later</button>
      </form>
    </section>

    <p class="hint">This is a static site: the controls are ready, but JavaScript has not given them behavior yet.</p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `index.html` in a browser. If you edit it, save the file and refresh the browser tab. The page will have structure, but it will look plain until you add the CSS.

### Read the important HTML pieces {.unnumbered}

- `<head>` holds information *about* the page. The browser-tab title and the CSS link belong there.
- `<body>` holds the parts people see and use.
- `<main>` groups the main content. Its `class="card"` gives CSS a useful name for this group.
- `<h1>` and `<h2>` are headings. `<p>` is a paragraph. `<ul>` and `<li>` make a list.
- `<section>` groups a related part of the page.
- `<img>` puts the local `gem.svg` picture on the page. Its `alt` text describes the picture for people who cannot see it.

## CSS basics: rules change how HTML looks

CSS is a list of rules. A rule starts with a **selector**—the HTML element or class that you want to style. Inside the braces, each **declaration** has a property, a colon, a value, and a semicolon.

```css
selector {
  property: value;
}
```

Read this rule aloud as: “For every element with the class `game-art`, make the border rounded.”

```css
.game-art {
  border-radius: 24px;
}
```

The dot is important. `.game-art` means “find `class="game-art"` in the HTML.” An element selector has no dot: `h1` styles every level-one heading and `img` styles every image. You can write more than one declaration inside the same braces.

| Selector | What it selects | Example use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `body` | the whole visible page | choose a default font and text color |
| `h1` | every main heading | make the title large and bold |
| `.intro` | elements with `class="intro"` | make the introduction italic |
| `.game-art` | the gem image with that class | set the image's frame and size |

## Style fonts and images with CSS

Save this in a second file named `styles.css`.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `styles.css`]{.code-label}

```css
:root {
  --ink: #17243b;
  --paper: #f7f4ff;
  --purple: #6d3df5;
  --yellow: #ffe48a;
}

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #c9efff, var(--paper));
  color: var(--ink);
  font-family: "Trebuchet MS", Verdana, sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

.card {
  width: min(92%, 620px);
  margin: 32px;
  padding: 32px;
  border: 4px solid var(--ink);
  border-radius: 24px;
  background: white;
  box-shadow: 10px 10px 0 var(--yellow);
}

.eyebrow {
  margin: 0;
  color: var(--purple);
  font-family: Verdana, sans-serif;
  font-size: 0.8rem;
  font-weight: 700;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
}

h1 {
  margin: 8px 0;
  color: var(--purple);
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 7vw, 3.5rem);
  font-weight: 800;
  line-height: 1.1;
}

.intro {
  color: #4c3f74;
  font-size: 1.15rem;
  font-style: italic;
}

.hint {
  font-size: 0.9rem;
}

.game-preview {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 22px;
  margin-top: 28px;
  padding: 18px;
  border: 2px solid #b7aee5;
  border-radius: 20px;
  background: #f2edff;
}

.game-preview h2 {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
}

.game-preview p {
  margin: 4px 0 0;
}

.game-art {
  width: 140px;
  height: 140px;
  padding: 14px;
  border: 4px solid var(--purple);
  border-radius: 24px;
  background: white;
  box-shadow: 7px 7px 0 var(--yellow);
  object-fit: contain;
}

section {
  margin-top: 28px;
  padding-top: 8px;
  border-top: 2px dashed #b7aee5;
}

form {
  display: grid;
  gap: 10px;
}

input,
select,
button {
  min-height: 44px;
  padding: 10px 12px;
  border: 2px solid var(--ink);
  border-radius: 10px;
  font: inherit;
}

.check-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 8px;
}

.check-row input {
  min-height: auto;
}

button {
  margin-top: 8px;
  background: var(--purple);
  color: white;
  cursor: pointer;
  font-weight: 800;
}

button:hover {
  background: #4d24c8;
}

input:focus-visible,
select:focus-visible,
button:focus-visible {
  outline: 4px solid var(--yellow);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

@media (max-width: 520px) {
  .game-preview {
    align-items: flex-start;
    flex-direction: column;
  }
}
```

### Give the site a readable voice {.unnumbered}

```css
body {
  font-family: "Trebuchet MS", Verdana, sans-serif;
}

h1 {
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 7vw, 3.5rem);
  font-weight: 800;
}

.intro {
  font-style: italic;
}
```

`font-family` chooses the lettering style. The comma-separated names are a **font stack**: the browser tries the first font and then tries the next one if needed. The last name, such as `sans-serif` or `serif`, is a broad backup family, so the page still has a sensible look on another computer.

`font-size` changes how large the letters appear. `font-weight` changes how thick they look: `400` is similar to normal text, while `700` is similar to bold. `font-style: italic` adds a slant for emphasis. Use the right HTML tag first—an `<h1>` should still be the main heading even if you later change its size with CSS.

### Frame an image with CSS {.unnumbered}

```css
.game-art {
  width: 140px;
  padding: 14px;
  border: 4px solid var(--purple);
  border-radius: 24px;
  box-shadow: 7px 7px 0 var(--yellow);
}
```

`width` keeps the image at a friendly size. `padding` adds breathing room inside its frame. `border` draws the edge, `border-radius` rounds the corners, and `box-shadow` makes the gem look as if it is resting above the card. Try changing `border-radius` to `50%`; the square frame becomes a circle.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Practice CSS one property at a time" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Change one value, save the CSS file, and refresh the browser. That small experiment tells you exactly which property made the difference. Helpful next references are the [W3Schools CSS tutorial](https://www.w3schools.com/css/), [CSS Fonts](https://www.w3schools.com/css/css_font.asp), and [CSS Styling Images](https://www.w3schools.com/css/css3_images.asp).

:::

## Prepare the inputs for JavaScript

The text box, menu, checkbox, and button are all **input elements**: parts of a page a person can use. Their labels make the controls easier to understand and help assistive technology describe them.

Look closely at this pair:

```html
<label for="player-name">Your game-maker name</label>
<input id="player-name" name="player-name" type="text">
```

The label's `for="player-name"` matches the input's `id="player-name"`. That connection means clicking the words “Your game-maker name” focuses the correct text box. The `id` will also let JavaScript find this exact element later.

The button uses `type="button"`. It looks and feels like a button, but it has no task yet. It will not submit the form or save the choices. JavaScript needs to listen for a click, read the inputs, and decide what to do.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Static does not mean unfinished" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Static pages are excellent for information, art portfolios, instructions, and game-planning pages. HTML gives them a sensible order; CSS makes them readable and expressive. JavaScript is only needed when the page must respond, calculate, remember, fetch data, or change while it is open.

The browser may remember what you typed for a moment, but this example has no code to save a player name. Refreshing or reopening the page can clear it. Code that remembers choices comes later.

:::
